title: Methodology
text: This page documents the research design, sample construction, and analytical decisions for Island Time, Interrupted. It explains what was done and why, including where judgments were made and what consequences those judgments carry for interpretation. The Data Dictionary explains what the data are and where they came from. The Technical Analysis shows the results.

title: Methodology
text:
Research Design

Questions
Primary: Was greater pre-pandemic dependence on international tourism associated with more severe 2020 GDP contractions among Caribbean, Pacific, and AIMS small island developing states?
Secondary: Were tourism-dependent economies more or less likely to have recovered to their 2019 real GDP levels by 2024?


Analytical approach
This is a cross-sectional exploratory analysis. The unit of analysis is the economy. The approach is descriptive and associational: does a pre-pandemic characteristic (tourism dependence) predict a 2020 outcome (GDP growth)? The statistical tool is bivariate OLS regression, supplemented by rank correlation and multiple specification comparisons.
This analysis does not establish causation. No controls are included for fiscal position, economic structure, pre-existing recession, pandemic-response policy, or population dynamics. The analysis is intentionally kept bivariate to maintain transparency — these are the raw patterns in the data before any further assumptions are introduced.

title: Methodology

Sample Definitions

Fixed-sample principle
Sample membership is determined by 2017–2019 indicator availability plus 2020 GDP growth availability. This definition is fixed and does not change when baseline windows are extended or narrowed. The 2017–2019 window was used for sample definition because it is the most recent pre-pandemic three-year period available for both indicators.

Excluded economies (and why)
Economies not in any shock sample are excluded because they lack either: - A usable pre-pandemic tourism baseline (AIA, GLP, MTQ, MSR, BES, COK, NIU: no WDI coverage; BLZ, TCA: no OWID vspend data for 2017–2019). - 2020 GDP growth data.
Exclusion is based on data availability, not substantive selection. These economies are documented in data/processed/country_coverage.csv.

title: Methodology
text:
Baseline Windows

Two specifications








Window
Years
Rationale




Primary (2015–2019)
Up to 5 years
Broader window, less sensitive to a single atypical year; more stable estimate of structural dependence


Sensitivity (2017–2019)
Up to 3 years
Most recent pre-pandemic conditions; used for sample-membership definition





Transparency about window selection
The 2015–2019 primary window was evaluated after observing the 2017–2019 results. This is not preregistered research. The primary specification was not selected before examining the data. This is documented explicitly, and both specifications are reported in full (see Analysis, Table A5). The two specifications produce nearly identical results for the OWID indicator.


Baseline construction
For each economy and each indicator, the baseline is the arithmetic mean of available annual observations within the window. A country with 4 out of 5 possible years contributes a 4-year mean. Medians are computed as supplementary statistics (in output tables) but are not used as primary regression inputs.
No imputation. Missing annual observations are not filled. Economies with zero observations in a window do not contribute a baseline.


Thin baselines
Economies with only one annual observation in the baseline window are flagged as “thin baseline” in all figures (open circles) and tables. Kiribati is the thin-baseline economy in both OWID vspend samples (1 observation in both 2015–2019 and 2017–2019). Sensitivity analyses excluding Kiribati show minimal effect on results.

title: Methodology
text:
Shock Model Specification

Outcome variable
2020 annual GDP growth (%) from WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG. This is the percentage change in constant-price GDP from 2019 to 2020.
Limitations: - Annual GDP growth aggregates a full calendar year. Travel restrictions began at different times in different economies; some may have had partial within-year recovery. - GDP growth does not capture unemployment, poverty, or debt accumulation. - Some economies had pre-existing recessions that overlap with the pandemic period.


Explanatory variable
Pre-pandemic tourism-dependence baseline (% of GDP or % of exports), computed as described above.


Estimation
Bivariate OLS: gdp_growth_2020 ~ baseline_tourism_dependence
This is the simplest possible linear specification. No interaction terms, no controls, no fixed effects. This is intentional: the goal is to describe the raw association transparently before introducing model complexity.


Eight principal models



Dimension
Levels




Indicator
OWID visitor spending (% GDP); WDI receipts (% exports)


Sample
OWID shock sample; WDI shock sample; Common sample


Window
2015–2019; 2017–2019



Models 1–4 use the 2015–2019 baseline; Models 5–8 use 2017–2019. All eight are reported. No model is suppressed. Model preference should not be inferred from which produces the most significant p-value.


Multiple comparison adjustment
Holm’s step-down procedure is applied across all 8 principal p-values. This is reported for transparency, not as a definitive decision criterion. The 8 models are not independent (overlapping samples and related outcomes), so the Holm adjustment is conservative.


Influential observations
Cook’s distance is computed for all models. The conventional threshold 4/N is used to flag influential observations. Maldives (MDV) is consistently the most influential in OWID models (Cook’s D ≈ 0.36–0.39). Timor-Leste (TLS) is influential in WDI receipts models.
Excluding influential observations is reported as a labeled diagnostic sensitivity analysis. Influential observations are not removed from primary models. The Maldives is an economically meaningful data point — an economy with genuine extreme tourism dependence that experienced one of the largest 2020 contractions.

title: Methodology
text:
Coverage-Restricted Sensitivity
A secondary sensitivity analysis restricts each sample to economies with at least 3 annual observations in the relevant baseline window. This tests whether thin-baseline economies drive the results.
The most consequential case is S5 (WDI receipts, 2017–2019, WDI sample, N=35 → 21): 14 economies are excluded because WDI 2019 receipts data is missing (the baseline can only be computed from 2017 and 2018). The restricted N=21 sample still shows a negative slope (−0.143) but with weaker evidence (p = 0.055). This primarily reflects the severe reduction in sample size rather than an absence of pattern.

title: Methodology
text:
Recovery Index

Construction
Recovery_index_t = (Real_GDP_t / Real_GDP_2019) × 100
Computed separately for aggregate real GDP (NY.GDP.MKTP.KD) and per-capita real GDP (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD). A value of 100 means the economy has exactly returned to its 2019 level; above 100 means it has exceeded it.


Pre-pandemic baseline: 2019
The reference year is 2019, the last full year before COVID-19 travel restrictions. This is the most natural pre-pandemic comparison point. 2015–2018 observations are included to show the pre-pandemic trend.


Comparison year: 2024
The primary recovery comparison year is 2024, the most recent year with near-complete data for the sample (28/29 economies; VIR has no 2024 data). 2025 data exists for 22 economies only, an insufficient base for cross-economy comparisons.
Annual sample sizes vary across the recovery period and are shown explicitly in figures (Overview Figure 3 and Analysis Figure 5). Cross-economy recovery comparisons at 2025 are not made because the 2025 sample (N=22) is not representative of the full shock sample.


Aggregate vs. per-capita distinction
These are not interchangeable. By 2024, 21 of 28 economies with available data had recovered aggregate real GDP to 2019 levels; 20 of 28 had recovered real GDP per capita. The net gap of one economy masks divergent dynamics in both directions: four economies (ATG, PNG, SYC, VUT) recovered aggregate but not per-capita GDP, consistent with population growth outpacing economic output; three economies (CUW, MHL, TUV) recovered per-capita but not aggregate GDP, consistent with declining or emigrating populations. Claims about recovery should specify which measure is being used.

text:
Reproduction

Software

R 4.4.1
Required packages: tidyverse, wbstats, here, scales, knitr, rmarkdown, patchwork, svglite



Script execution order
source("R/01_data_acquisition.R")   # ~2-3 min; calls World Bank API
source("R/02_data_quality.R")
source("R/03_preliminary_eda.R")
source("R/04_shock_models.R")
source("R/05_recovery_analysis.R")


Rendering the site
quarto render
This renders all four pages to docs/. The site is published from docs/ on the main branch via GitHub Pages.


World Bank API
WDI data is retrieved using wbstats::wb_data(). Future runs may retrieve updated data (particularly as WDI receipts lag resolves and 2025 real GDP estimates become final). The current retrieval date and returned codes are recorded in data/raw/worldbank/wdi_retrieval_metadata.txt. Note that ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS (tourism receipts) contains no observations beyond 2020 in this retrieval; this appears to reflect a change in UN Tourism data dissemination rather than a simple publication lag, and may indicate the WDI series is no longer actively updated.


OWID data
OWID CSV files in data/raw/ are fixed downloads from January–July 2026. They will not automatically update. To retrieve updated data, download fresh CSVs from the OWID grapher and replace the files in data/raw/.

title: Technical Analysis
text: This page documents the analytical evidence behind the Overview. It covers sample construction, tourism indicator coverage, all eight principal shock-model estimates, robustness diagnostics, and economic recovery through 2024. Code is available via the fold buttons. Source documentation and variable definitions are in the Data Dictionary; research design and methodological decisions are in Methodology.

None of the seven WDI-absent economies qualifies for any shock or recovery sample.

title: Technical Analysis
text:
Tourism Indicator Coverage
Data availability differs substantially between the two principal indicators. The OWID visitor spending series has near-complete coverage through 2024; the WDI receipts series stops at 2020 and is missing 2019 data for 14 of 35 WDI-sample members. This coverage asymmetry is part of why the two indicators produce different results.

Coverage matrix








Figure 1: Data coverage matrix across the candidate universe. Green = all requested years available; yellow = partial (one year); grey = absent.







WDI receipts: end of series in this retrieval
WDI ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS has no observations beyond 2020 in the retrieved data. This does not appear to be a simple publication lag; it likely reflects a change in UN Tourism’s data dissemination approach following the pandemic. The pre-pandemic coverage is also uneven: 14 of 35 WDI sample members have no 2019 receipts observation, meaning their 2017–2019 baseline draws on 2017 and 2018 only. The OWID visitor spending series, by contrast, is available through 2024 with near-complete coverage.

title: Technical Analysis
text:
Indicator Comparison
The two principal measures are correlated but not equivalent. Figure 2 shows the relationship between them across the 24-economy common sample.








Figure 2: OWID visitor spending (% GDP) vs. WDI tourism receipts (% exports), 2015–2019 averages. The two indicators are correlated but not interchangeable — they divide by different denominators and measure related but distinct economic concepts.





The Pearson correlation between the two indicators (across economies with both) is approximately 0.77, and the Spearman rank correlation is 0.86. They produce similar rankings but material differences for some economies. The WDI receipts/exports denominator amplifies the apparent dependence of export-intensive small economies, while the OWID visitor spending/GDP denominator captures the share of overall economic activity attributable to visitors.

Recovery vs. tourism dependence








Figure 6: Pre-pandemic visitor spending vs. 2024 real GDP index (2019=100). No statistically significant association (Pearson r = 0.21, p = 0.27, N = 28).





The absence of a significant association between pre-pandemic tourism dependence and the 2024 recovery index (Figure 6) does not mean tourism dependence was harmless or that the initial shock was inconsequential for these economies. Rather, the relationship between pre-pandemic exposure and longer-term economic recovery is not straightforward. Although tourism-dependent economies experienced particularly severe contractions in 2020, their subsequent recovery trajectories varied. By 2024, the degree of pre-pandemic tourism dependence alone did not explain which economies had regained their 2019 aggregate GDP levels.
Per-capita recovery provides a more nuanced picture. By 2024, 20 of 28 economies had recovered their 2019 real GDP per capita, compared with 21 of 28 for aggregate GDP. The difference illustrates why aggregate output alone can overstate the extent of economic recovery: an economy may regain its total output while remaining below its pre-pandemic level on a per-person basis. Population growth is one possible contributor to this divergence, although this analysis does not isolate its effects.

See Data Dictionary for source documentation and Methodology for research design.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
For most countries, a pandemic is a health crisis with economic side effects. For a small island economy built on international tourism, the equation is different. When COVID-19 closed borders in early 2020 and global arrivals fell by roughly 74 percent, the interruption of travel was not a disruption to one sector of the economy — in many places, it was closer to the interruption of the economy itself.
The question this analysis asks is a simple one: Were small island economies that depended more on international tourism before the pandemic more severely affected in 2020?
The answer, for the best available measure of tourism dependence, is yes. But the more interesting question — what happened next — turns out to have a considerably less tidy answer.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
For most countries, a pandemic is a health crisis with economic side effects. For a small island economy built on international tourism, the equation is different. When COVID-19 closed borders in early 2020 and global arrivals fell by roughly 74 percent, the interruption of travel was not a disruption to one sector of the economy — in many places, it was closer to the interruption of the economy itself.
The question this analysis asks is a simple one: Were small island economies that depended more on international tourism before the pandemic more severely affected in 2020?
The answer, for the best available measure of tourism dependence, is yes. But the more interesting question — what happened next — turns out to have a considerably less tidy answer.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
Who Was Most Exposed?
Not all island economies are equally dependent on tourism. The range, even within a 29-economy sample drawn from the Caribbean, Pacific, and AIMS regions, is striking.








Figure 1: International visitor spending as a share of GDP, 2015–2019 average. Each bar is one economy in the primary shock sample (N = 29). Open circle indicates Kiribati, which has only one year of pre-pandemic data.





At one extreme: Aruba and Maldives, with international visitor spending averaging roughly 60 and 59 percent of GDP over 2015–2019. Antigua and Barbuda and Sint Maarten were not far behind. At the other end: Guinea-Bissau, Trinidad and Tobago, Suriname — economies where tourism is a real sector but not the economic foundation.
An economy where foreign visitors account for 60 percent of GDP is structurally different from one where they account for 5 percent. When travel stopped, those differences mattered enormously.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
Measuring Exposure
Two indicators of tourism dependence are used in this analysis, and they are not interchangeable.
The primary measure is international visitor spending as a share of GDP — how much international tourists spend in a country relative to the size of that country’s economy. This comes from UN Tourism statistics processed by Our World in Data and is available for all 29 economies in the primary sample. High values mean a large fraction of economic activity depends directly on people arriving from abroad.
The complementary measure is international tourism receipts as a share of total exports, from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators. This asks a related but different question: how important are tourism earnings relative to everything else the economy sells to the rest of the world? For countries with limited other exports, the two measures can tell very different stories about the same destination.
The analysis uses the first measure as primary and the second as a check. The comparison between them turns out to be part of the story — not just methodological housekeeping.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
The 2020 Shock








Figure 2: Pre-pandemic visitor spending (2015–2019 average) versus 2020 real GDP growth. The OLS line describes the cross-sectional association across the 29-economy sample. It is exploratory; it does not establish causation. Open circle: Kiribati. Sources: OWID / UN Tourism; WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG.





The slope is visible without the regression line: across these 29 economies, the more of an economy’s activity depended on international visitors before the pandemic, the worse 2020 GDP growth tended to be.
Fitting a simple regression, each additional percentage point of visitor spending relative to GDP was associated with roughly 0.31 percentage points of additional contraction in 2020. The relationship explains about 41% of the variation in 2020 growth rates across the sample (R² = 0.414, p < 0.001). For a bivariate cross-sectional relationship across 29 diverse economies, that is a substantial share of explained variation.

The Maldives and what it tells us
The Maldives deserves a specific note. With visitor spending averaging about 59 percent of GDP and a GDP contraction of roughly 33 percent in 2020, it sits at the far extreme of both axes — the most tourism-dependent economy in the sample and the most severely affected. It is also the most statistically influential single observation.
Excluding the Maldives reduces R² from 0.414 to approximately 0.31, but the negative association remains statistically significant (p = 0.002). The finding does not depend on a single outlier. The Maldives is an unusually clear example of the relationship, not the reason it exists.
The result also holds when the 2017–2019 average replaces the 2015–2019 baseline (slope = -0.32, R² = 0.428) and when the analysis is restricted to the 24 economies with data for both tourism indicators (R² = 0.489).
This is an observational analysis of 29 economies. It documents an association, not a mechanism. Pre-existing fiscal pressures, the timing of border closures, domestic economic alternatives, and many other factors are not controlled for. The pattern is consistent with the economic logic of tourism dependence, but consistent-with is not the same as explained-by.


The other indicator tells a more complicated story
The World Bank’s tourism receipts measure — receipts as a share of total exports — produces weaker and less consistent results. In the full WDI sample of 35 economies, the relationship falls just short of conventional statistical thresholds (R² = 0.1, p = 0.064). In the 24-economy common sample — the same countries analyzed with both indicators — the relationship is more evident but explains considerably less of the variation (R² = 0.233).
This matters. The choice of how to measure tourism dependence is not a purely technical question. The two indicators cover different countries, divide by different denominators, and in the common sample produce R² values of 0.489 versus 0.233. Whether pre-pandemic tourism dependence appears strongly associated with the 2020 shock depends partly on how you measure it. The Technical Analysis documents all eight model specifications; none is hidden.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
Recovery: Messier Than the Shock








Figure 3: Real GDP trajectories, 2015–2025. Index: 2019 = 100. Each line is one economy in the primary shock sample, coloured by region. Numbers at the bottom of each panel show how many economies have data in that year. Source: WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD (constant 2015 USD). 2025 figures are preliminary for a subset of economies.





By 2024, 21 of 28 economies with available data had returned to or exceeded their 2019 aggregate real GDP. The pattern for most of them looked something like a steep V: a sharp drop in 2020, a partial recovery in 2021, and a return to baseline within two or three years.
But counting heads at a single comparison year conceals a more complex picture.

Two kinds of recovery, and they’re not the same
Aggregate GDP and GDP per capita tell different stories, particularly in small island economies where population dynamics — emigration, population growth, aging — can move significantly over just a few years.
Of the 28 economies with 2024 real GDP data:

20 of 28 had recovered real GDP per capita to 2019 levels — one fewer than the aggregate count.

The gap between the two measures runs in both directions. Four economies — Seychelles, Antigua & Barbuda, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu — had restored total GDP but not GDP per capita by 2024. This pattern is consistent with population growth outpacing economic recovery: total output returned, but per-person output had not. Three economies — Curaçao, Marshall Islands, Tuvalu — showed the opposite: GDP per capita had recovered, but total output had not. This is consistent with declining or emigrating populations, where per-person output can rise even when the aggregate shrinks.
7 economies had not recovered aggregate GDP to 2019 levels by 2024: Suriname, Cuba, Tuvalu, Trinidad & Tobago, Marshall Islands, Curaçao, Solomon Islands. Several of these — particularly Cuba, Suriname, and Trinidad and Tobago — faced economic difficulties that predated the pandemic.


Tourism dependence did not predict the recovery
Here the story departs from what the shock analysis might suggest. Among these 28 economies, pre-pandemic tourism dependence was not significantly associated with where an economy stood relative to its 2019 GDP level in 2024 (Pearson r = 0.21, p = 0.275). Pre-pandemic tourism dependence, while informative about initial exposure, tells us relatively little about where an economy stood four years later.
The reason this relationship is absent is worth understanding, not dismissing. The same mechanism that drove the initial shock also drove the subsequent rebound. Economies where visitor spending accounts for 50–60 percent of GDP contracted sharply in 2020 when travel stopped — and then recovered sharply from 2021 onward as travel resumed. Looking only at where they ended up in 2024 relative to 2019, the two phases roughly cancel out.
This is not evidence that tourism-dependent islands are resilient. It is evidence that aggregate GDP at a single comparison year is an incomplete measure of what an economy actually experienced between 2020 and 2024. The employment lost, the debt accumulated to bridge the gap, the businesses that did not survive: none of that is captured in whether a GDP index crossed the 100 threshold.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
The Central Argument
The 2020 economic shock in small island developing states was not random, and it was not uniform. It tracked — with considerable regularity across three ocean regions — how much of an economy’s activity depended on international visitors.
That association is strong enough to be visible in the data, stable across different baseline windows and sample compositions, and not dependent on a single influential observation. It is consistent with the economic structure of tourism dependence. What it cannot do, by itself, is explain the specific trajectory of any particular economy — those depend on fiscal buffers, policy choices, and factors that a simple cross-sectional comparison cannot untangle.
The recovery, by contrast, was not neatly structured by prior exposure. Most island economies regained their pre-pandemic GDP levels within a few years. Some had not by 2024. The differences appear to reflect country-specific circumstances that tourism dependence alone does not predict.
Two things emerge from this. First, pre-pandemic visitor spending as a share of GDP is a meaningful indicator of economic exposure to travel-disruption shocks. Second, the size of an economy’s initial shock tells you surprisingly little about where it ends up four years later.
The full picture requires looking at individual trajectories, not just the cross-sectional pattern.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
This page documents every data source, variable, and processed dataset used in the analysis. For how the data were used — sample construction, baseline calculations, model specifications — see Methodology. For the analysis itself, see Technical Analysis.
Most important distinction: the OWID visitor spending indicator and the WDI tourism receipts indicator are not interchangeable. They divide by different denominators, cover different economies, and have different data availability. The analysis uses them as separate measures of related but distinct aspects of tourism dependence.

Tourism Indicators

OWID International Visitor Spending (% of GDP)







Field
Value




Short name
OWID visitor spending


Variable name in analysis
visitor_spend_gdp_pct, baseline vspend_mean_1519 / vspend_mean_1719


Definition
Money received by the destination country from foreign visitors, including spending on accommodation, food, transport, entertainment, shopping, and fares paid to the country’s own airlines, expressed as a percentage of GDP


Units
Percent of GDP


Source
UN Tourism (2025); National statistical organizations and central banks, OECD national accounts, and World Bank staff estimates (2026) — processed by Our World in Data


OWID variable ID
1146095


Date range
1995–2024


Coverage
~200 countries/territories


Raw file
data/raw/spending-by-international-visitors-while-visiting-a-country-as-a-share-of-gdp/



This indicator does not correspond to a single WDI indicator code. The numerator (international tourism receipts) comes from UN Tourism statistics collected through annual questionnaires following the International Recommendations for Tourism Statistics (IRTS 2008). The denominator (GDP) comes from World Bank national accounts estimates. Do not attribute this indicator to ST.INT.XPND.GD.ZS or any other unverified WDI code.
Distinction from tourism direct GDP: Visitor spending captures money spent by foreign visitors in a country. This is not equivalent to tourism’s direct contribution to GDP. A dollar spent by a visitor does not translate into a dollar of domestic value added — a portion flows to imported goods and services. Tourism direct GDP (SDG 8.9.1) measures the domestic value-added component only; it is a smaller number and requires Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) methodology to calculate.
Use in analysis: Primary pre-pandemic tourism-dependence indicator. 2015–2019 five-year means used as the primary baseline; 2017–2019 three-year means used as a sensitivity comparison.

Field
Value




Short name

Variable name

Definition
Tourism Direct GDP as a share of total GDP. Measures the value created when visitors spend money in the country, expressed as gross value added by all industries serving visitors, plus net taxes on goods and services tourists buy. Tracks SDG 8.9.1.


Units
Percent of GDP


Source

Methodology
Tourism Satellite Account (TSA). Countries without a TSA are absent from this dataset — coverage gaps reflect institutional capacity, not absence of tourism.

2008–2023


Coverage
~125 countries with TSA data


Raw file
data/raw/tourism-gdp-proportion-of-total-gdp/



Not used as primary indicator in this analysis due to substantially lower coverage (15 of 29 OWID shock sample members have TSA data, vs. 29/29 for the visitor spending indicator). Used as a complementary measure in coverage audits.

This is a volume measure, not an economic dependence indicator. It does not appear in the primary shock regression. It is included in the data for contextual reference.



WDI International Tourism Receipts (% of Total Exports)







Field
Value

WDI tourism receipts


WDI code
ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS

Definition
International tourism receipts as a percentage of total exports of goods and services. Tourism receipts include any payments made to the destination country by tourists for accommodation, food, transport, entertainment, and shopping during their visit.

World Development Indicators, World Bank

~1995–2020 in this retrieval (no observations beyond 2020)

~180 countries

wbstats::wb_data(), November 2026



Note on availability: this series ends at 2020 in the current retrieval. WDI ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS contains no observations beyond 2020 in the November 2026 retrieval. The most likely explanation is a change in UN Tourism’s data dissemination approach following the pandemic — much of UN Tourism’s current reporting has moved to interactive data portals — rather than a simple publication lag. The WDI series may no longer be actively updated. Additionally, 2019 data is missing for 14 of 35 WDI shock-sample members — their 2017–2019 baseline is computed from 2017 and 2018 only. Users requiring post-pandemic tracking of tourism receipts should consult the UN Tourism data portal directly.
Distinction from OWID visitor spending: Both series ultimately draw on UN Tourism receipts data, but:

The denominator differs: OWID uses GDP; WDI uses total exports of goods and services.
Their magnitudes and rankings differ accordingly: for export-intensive micro-states, the receipts/exports ratio can be very large; for larger, more diversified economies, it can be small.
The two series are correlated (Pearson r ≈ 0.77, Spearman ρ ≈ 0.86 across the common sample) but not interchangeable.

Use in analysis: Complementary indicator. Used in WDI shock sample (N=35) and common-sample comparison alongside OWID visitor spending.

Processed Datasets

data/processed/candidates.csv
58-economy candidate universe. Fields: iso3, country, sids_region, sids_status, political_status, source, notes. Authority: UN-OHRLLS list of SIDS, November 2026.


data/processed/country_coverage.csv
Coverage matrix. One row per candidate (58 rows). Fields include observation counts for each indicator in the 2017–2019 window and binary sample-membership flags (in_primary_shock_sample, in_receipts_shock_sample, in_common_sample, in_recovery_sample).


data/processed/baseline_shock_recovery.csv
One row per economy that appears in the analytical panel (57 economies). Contains: 2015–2019 and 2017–2019 baseline means and observation counts for all tourism indicators; 2015–2025 wide-format columns for economic outcomes; sample membership flags. BES is absent because it has no data in any source.


data/processed/analytical_panel.csv
Long-format, unbalanced panel. 1,707 rows; 57 economies; years 1995–2025 (coverage varies by indicator and economy). All WDI and OWID indicators are present as columns; most rows have NA for at least some indicators. This is not a balanced panel: not every economy has observations for every year. Used as the primary input to baseline and recovery calculations. BES is absent (no data in any source).


data/processed/recovery_index.csv
Long-format recovery dataset for primary shock sample (N = 29), years 2015–2025. Contains gdp_index (real GDP, 2019 = 100) and gdppc_index (real GDP per capita, 2019 = 100). 2025 rows exist for 22 of 29 economies (preliminary estimates).

SIDS Classification



Table D1. SIDS universe classification notes.






topic

UN SIDS count
UN-OHRLLS lists 39 economies under Small Island Developing States. Of these, 37 are UN General Assembly member states; Cook Islands and Niue are sovereign states in free association with New Zealand and are not UNGA members but ARE included on the SIDS list.


Bahrain (BHR)
Was previously on some UN SIDS lists as an AIMS economy. As of the current UN-OHRLLS list (retrieved November 2026), Bahrain is not listed as a SIDS. Not included in the candidate universe.


Associate Members
The 18 associate members listed by UN-OHRLLS are territories and dependencies that are associate members of UN Regional Commissions. They are included in the SIDS group but are not sovereign states. Not all have WDI coverage.


BES
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are Dutch special municipalities. Not on the UN-OHRLLS list. Retained in the candidate universe as an other island economy for regional completeness. No WDI coverage and does not contribute to any analytical sample.

UN-OHRLLS list of SIDS, retrieved November 2026. URL: https://www.un.org/ohrlls/content/list-sids
